NEW PRESIDENT OF EXECUTIVE COUNCIL
By Edward C. Peattie, Phi '06
ON JANUARY 16, 1956, Benjamin T.
Burton, Chi '21, was elected Presi
dent of the Executive Council of Psi Upsi
lon. He succeeded to this position which
has been in the capable hands of LeRoy J.
Weed, Theta '01, since October 8, 1946.
Ben served as Second Vice-President
from May 8, 1939, to October 8, 1940,
and from October 8, 1940, to January 16,
1956, as Vice-President, and has been a
member of the Executive Council since
1935. In college, he was a member of the
honorary Junior Society of Alpha, Samack,
and the Honorary Senior Society, Sphinx
Head, and was one of the organizers of
the Red Key Society which has since
grown to be the undergraduate organiza
tion charged with the responsibility of
entertaining visiting teams.
During World War I he served as 2nd
Lieutenant in Field Artillery at Camp
Zachary Taylor, Louisville, Kentucky.
Brother Burton and Brother Charles K.
Dickson, Chi '21, while undergraduates
attended a dance at Wells CoUege and
there met their future wives. In 1923 he
married Miss Mary Pew of Philadelphia,
daughter of the late John G. Pew, pioneer
oil, gas and shipbuilding executive and
philanthropist.
Brother Burton's three daughters are:
Dr. Sarah Burton Nelson, Wells College,
1946, and Cornell Medical School, 1950.
Her husband. Major Nelson, was at West
Point, a classmate and good friend of
President Eisenhower's son.
Mary Burton Blackney�Scripps Col
lege, Cahfomia, 1950, where she stood
first in her class and was
Queen of the
May, and appeared in Life Magazine.
Barbara Carol Burton�
currently attend
ing Cornell School of Nursing. She for
merly attended Northwestern University
and Wells College.
Brother Burton's firm is now Burton,
Dana and Company, with offices in New
York, Philadelphia and Washington. He
is senior partner of this brokerage firm.
He is a member of the Bankers' Club
of America, Downtown Athletic Club,
Racquet Club of Philadelphia, Union
League Club of New York, Cornell Club
of New York, Montclair Golf Club. Ben
Burton is Past Secretary and Treasurer of
the Chi of Psi Upsilon, and served as its
President for five years. In the interim he
has also been President of his 1921 class
and President of the Cornell Club of Essex
County (New Jersey). He also played an
important part in raising twelve million
dollars for Cornell in one
year as VicePresident of the Cornell Alumni Fund.
Returning to his undergraduate days,
he was
Manager of the Cornell crew, the
last to be coached by the famous "Pop"
Courtney.
Let us not forget his earnest work, in
cluding five years as President of the Psi
Upsilon Alumni Association. His faithful
attendance at Council meetings and Con
ventions is just one more indication of his
interest in Psi Upsilon.
In short, Brother Burton has proved a
thorough believer in his slogan of the Chi,
"Give a
thought daily to Cornell and the
Chi." For Ben Burton a more
appropriate
slogan might be, "Give a
thought daily to
your Alma Mater, your Fratemity, and
your Community."

ma '96, died at the New Rochelle Hos

A former member of the Executive

of Trustees of Amherst College, and for
many years until his death President of the
Gamma Chapter Corporation, Brother
Fales was one of the Gamma's most dis
tinguished, well-loved and loyal sons. His
long and devoted service to his college and
his fraternity, and the high regard and
affection in which he was held by genera

Paul D. Weathers, Gamma '15, and
adopted by the Gamma Chapter Corpora
tion at its

"Frederick Sayward Fales, for sixty-two

of Psi UpsUon, for thirty-three years a

FRATERNITIES AND SORORITIES
By A. Blair Knapp, Pi '26, President of Denison College
A. Blair Knapp,
PI '26
Editor's note: We be
lieve this significant
article by A. Blair
Knapp, Pi '26, former
Treasurer of the Execu
tive Council of Psi Up
silon, will be of interest
to members of the Fra
ternity.
Brother Knapp was
recipient of the honor
ary doctor of humane
letters degree at a
special convocation at Trinity College, Hart
ford, Conn., Sunday, Nov. 13, 1955. The de
gree was one of 14 conferred by President
Albert C. Jacobs, Phi '21, climaxing a
four-day
fall convocation on the theme, "The Challenge
to Liberal Education." The speaker was Carlos
P. Romulo, Philippines' Ambassador to the
United Nations.
President Knapp was one of the speakers,
appearing on the second evening's program.
Dr. Knapp holds a similar honorary degree
from Temple University, Philadelphia, Pa.,
where he was
serving as vice president when
he accepted his present appointment. That
degree was conferred in 1952. His first honor
ary degree, that of doctor of laws, was con
ferred by his alma mater, Syracuse University,
on his appointment to the Denison presidency.
The citation for the new
degree reads in
part: "He is deeply engaged in many activities
that foster the sound education of our
youth."
Brother Knapp has been advanced to the
chairmanship of the Commission on Student
Personnel of the American Council on Edu
cation, of which he has been a member since
1952. The same
year he was
appointed to the
advisory board of the U.S. National Student
Association. The following year he was made
council member-at-large of the Association of
College Honor Societies.
The year Brother Knapp joined the Denison
administrative staff he was
president of the
National Association of Student Personnel Ad
ministrators. In 1953-54 he was
president of
the Ohio Foundation of Independent Colleges,
Inc., and since then has been a member of the
executive board.
Brother Knapp is married to the former
Gertrude Park of Syracuse, N.Y. They have
an invalid son, Richard, and daughter, Susan.
WHAT
about fraternities and sororities
at Denison? This is a
question which
I frequently get in one form or another
from alumni, parents, and others interested
in Denison. I presume that the question
is prompted more often than not by the
growing criticism of fraternities and sorori
ties in many parts of the country and in
many different other institutions. If I were
a
president of a
completely new institu
tion and I had the privilege of determining
whether or not fraternities and sororities
should be part of that institution, I frankly
do not know what my decision would be.
There are, of course, both great ad
vantages and problems in the fraternity
and sorority system. I have also always
been impressed with the fact that institu
tions without fraternities and sororities
seem to have some of the same
problems
although the forms which they take may
be different. In any event, Denison is not
a new institution and fraternities and so
rorities have been part of its Iffe for a
long time.
The basic answer to this question has
always been, therefore, that it is up to the
coUege to see to it that fraternities' and
sororities produce for us more of the ad
vantages and fewer of the problems. In
other words, so far as I am concerned, the
obligation is not to enter into any con
troversy as to whether we
ought to have
them or not to, but to provide leadership
to see to it that they contribute as much
as
possible to the objective of the institu
tion.
Under Attack Today
There can be no
question but that fra
temities and sororities are under greater
attack today than they have been for some
time. It is alleged that their influence on
many campuses is anti-intellectual; they
are
charged with being anti-democratic
because of the criteria used in the selec
tive process; they are even more
frequently
charged with being a divisive influence on
40

the diamond of psi upsilon 41
campus, making the development of an
all-college community attitude and loyal
ties more difficult. Of late, there have been
published criticisms alleging that the local
chapters of national fraternities and sorori
ties are under the domination of the na
tional officers whose concepts of education
are
frequently at odds with faculty and
administrators of individual colleges.
So far as the Denison campus is con
cerned, these charges do not
apply, at
least in their full impHcation. There have
been anti-intellectual attitudes developed
from time to time by Denison chapters.
I cannot
deny that one
chapter or another
has at a
given moment been guilty of anti
democratic decisions; I would have to
admit that there are times when fraternity
and sorority membership seems to take
ascendency over the Alma Mater, but that
these three characteristics are
typical of
the fraternities and sororities as a whole,
I think I must deny.
What is forgotten in the sweeping gen
eralizations on fraternities and sororities
and the attacks on them is the fact that
chapters of a
given fraternity vary greatly
from each other from coUege to college.
On a
given campus they also vary greatly
from each other from year to year. Leader
ship within the chapter is constantly chang
ing. Given strong leadership with real in
sight as to the real place of the chapter
in the Hfe of the college, these charges
are not apt to be true. Given indifferent or
irresponsible leadership, as
groups are
bound to
get on occasion, these and other
criticisms become pertinent.
Duty to Shape Attitudes
My position is that the college faculty
and administration have the responsibihty
to influence chapter leadership in bringing
about the kind of chapter attitudes which
are desired. Admittedly, there are sound
criticisms of the rushing and selective
processes used here. No one is more con
scious of these weaknesses than the so
rority and fraternity leaders. No one is
working harder to correct them. Our job
is to aid where we can in strengthening
the hand of these leaders who have insight
into the problem rather than issue any
administrative or
faculty edicts that pres
ent practices shall be changed. There are
times when one fears that loyalty to fra
ternities has somewhat overcome
loyalty
to Alma Mater, but in my experience
here, these occasions are not experienced
often and tend to be fleeting. When there
is really an
all-college problem, we turn
with confidence to the fraternity leader
ship, both undergraduate and alumni.
I have always felt that one of the great
mistakes that has been made by faculties
and administrators in dealing with fra
ternities and sororities has been to turn
too quickly to the authoritarian ultimatum.
We much prefer to
try to strengthen the
hand of student leadership in all these
areas of difficulty, confident that if we do
so the undergraduates will provide the
right answers.
What I have been trying to
say per
haps can be summarized briefly. Fraterni
ties and sororities at Denison have been
an
integral part of this college for a
long
time. The contributions have been great.
There are weaknesses, and from time to
time there are real difficulties. Our experi
ence, however, indicates that the best
course to overcome the difficulties is to
work with chapter leaders to strengthen
their hand. Our experience thus far is that
this method of operation pays great divi
dends.
